text:
JS 1012

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-12-259142-010

DATE:

November 22, 2002

______________________________________________________________________

By:

THE HONOURABLE

MARIE ST-PIERRE, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

N... B...

Applicant/Defendant

v.

S... V...

Defendant/Petitioner

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

The parties, N... B... (
B...
) and S...
V... (
V...
), were married on February 12, 1988 in Pakistan.  Both were,
and still are, citizens of Pakistan.

[
2
]

B... and V... have two children: a son, Sh...
who was borned in Pakistan on […], 1990 and a daughter, S..., who was borned in
the United States on […], 1995.

[
3
]

From February 12, 1988 to the end of 1994, the
family has lived in Pakistan.

[
4
]

In 1994, further to various research,
consultations and verifications, B... and V... decided, for their sakes and
their children's sakes, to leave Pakistan and to try to immigrate to North
America.

[
5
]

From December 1994 to August 1996, they have
lived in the United States (Florida) where they could not obtain immigration
status.  Therefore, in August 1996, they moved to Montreal, Canada.

[
6
]

While living in Montreal, they made claims to be
recognized as "Convention refugee":  their claims were denied
(exhibit R-5).  An application for employment authorization, a review of the
case in accordance with the PDRCC class definition, and a request for
Ministerial exemption changed nothing (exhibit R-5).  A removal order was
issued on July 5,1999.  The family left Montreal for Haiti wherefrom B...
obtained a work permit to work as information system date processing manager
for S... Inc.  The family came back to Montreal where it is still living as of
this day.  The conditions of B...'s work permit are (exhibit R-6) :

« EMPLOYER                    :           S...
INC.

OCCUPATION    :           INFO SYST DATE PROCESSING MGRS

TERMS AND CONDITIONS:

1. PROHIBITED FROM ATTENDING ANY EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTION    AND TAKING ANY
ACADEMIC, PROFESSIONAL OR VOCATIONAL TRAINING COURSE.

2. NOT AUTHORIZED TO WORK IN ANY OCCUPATION OTHER THAN STATED.

3. NOT AUTHORIZED TO  WORK FOR ANY EMPLOYER OTHER THAN STATED.

4. NOT AUTHORIZED TO WORK IN ANY LOCATION OTHER THAN STATED.

5. MUST LEAVE CANADA BY 30 NOV 2002»

[
7
]

The family has also filed for immigration
through Mexico where their Canadian immigration file is still pending.  The
Court will come back to that later in her judgement.

[
8
]

In January 2001, the marriage broke down.

[
9
]

From the court file and the proof that was made
before the Court last week, it appears that the breakdown of the marriage is
due to irreconcilable differences:  physical violence, moral violence and adultery

may be part of
said differences. However unless it has to, given
the issues before her to which the Court will come back later on, the Court is
not to decide, has not to decide and will not decide if that is so: under the

Divorce Act
, the custodial
parent's conduct can be considered only if
relevant to his or her ability to act as parent of the child.

[
10
]

The parties agreed to mediation.  Six meetings
where held (May 15 and 22, June 5, 12, 19, 26, 2001)  and, through such
mediation, the parties came to an agreement concerning any and all provisional
and accessory measures to their separation and divorce.

[
11
]

It was namely agreed between the parties:

•

that V... would continue to live in the
apartment which had been occupied, until then, by all members of the family and
that B... would find himself an other apartment, nearby :  the parties acted
accordingly as of July 1, 2001.

•

that they were both good parent.

•

that, in the best interests of their children,
they would share custody (50%-50%).

[
12
]

Like marriage itself, such an agreement, if it
is to succeed, has to be worked out by two persons who are determined, on their
own will and in good faith, to make it work.

[
13
]

On August 15, 2001,  B... brought an application
for divorce asking the court to grant a judgment of divorce, to confirm the
agreement of the parties as to corollary relief and to order them to respect
its terms the whole without costs. He also brought a motion for provisional
measures to confirm the agreement.

[
14
]

On January 24, 2002, a consent was signed by
both parties and their respective counsel, under the terms and conditions
previously agreed upon through mediation, whereby the parties accepted and
stipulated, namely :

«
AGREEMENT ON PROVISIONAL
MEASURES AND ACCESSORY MEASURES OF THE DIVORCE

WHEREAS
the applicant (B...) filed a declaration in divorce before this
court;

WHEREAS
the parties have discuss and settled their differences in
mediation;

WHEREAS
the parties have decided to signed an agreement on the provisional
measures and accessory measures to their divorce;

WHEREAS
the applicant (B...) filed a motion in provisional measures before
this court;

1.         The preamble is part of the present agreement;

3.         They have both accepted that they will live under the
conditions enumerated herein under until such time that they received the final
court judgement;

5.         The parties declare that they have two children namely,
Sh... B... born on […] 1990 and S... B... born […], 1995;

6.         The parties agreed to settle through mediation the
remaining issues arising out of the family patrimony, the division of the
assets and liabilities, the principal residence of their children and parental
authority, access rights to their children, and the child support and
alimentary pensions;

8.         The parties declare that they are consulting with
independent legal counsel;

11.1
Parental authority

The
parents reconfirm that it is in the best interest of their children that they
maintain at all times a good relationship with both parents.  They understand
the importance of the image that their children have of their parents and thus
undertake to show no disrespect towards the other parent in the presence of
their children.  They mutually recognise each other parental competency and
will both continue to assume their parental authority concerning the children.
They will consult for all important decisions concerning their children's
education, health, and welfare.  They will exchange all important information
with the other parent so as to permit an adequate involvement of each parent in
their children's development.  Each parent shall make the necessary day to day
decisions concerning the children while they are in their custody.

11.2
Residence

11.2.1  The residences of their children shall be both parents.

11.2.2

The children shall reside with each parent according to the
following schedule:

➢

Week one:  Sunday night, Monday, Tuesday                      with
mother

Tuesday night, Wednesday, Thursday            with father

Thursday night, Friday, Saturday, Sunday       with mother

➢

Week two:  Sunday night, Monday, Tuesday                      with
father

Tuesday night, Wednesday, Thursday            with mother

Thursday night, Friday, Saturday, Sunday       with father

This schedule to alternate
throughout the year except for holidays and vacation periods.

11.2.4  Both parents agree that they will live within the same
school district while their children are attending elementary school;

11.2.5  They further agree that neither parent will move more than
50 kilometres from "downtown Montreal" without the consent of the
other parent and the children once they have reached 13 years of age.  If a
parent moves outside this area, without the consent of the other, they forfeit
their custodial/residential rights.

11.3
Visitation rights

11.3.1  The non-custodial parent will have liberal access to the
children at all times, as long as said access does not interfere with
established plans of the custodial parent.  Neither parent shall take their
children out of the country without the prior written consent of the other, which
shall not be unduly withheld;

11.3.4  If a parent is out of town when they would normally have
their children then the children shall reside with the parent that is in town
unless the receiving parent can not accept the children or both parents are out
of town for an extended time then the responsible parent will make the
appropriate arrangements;

11.3.7  The grandparents with the parents' consent shall have access
rights with their grand children;

11.3.8  The parents shall make sure that their children are returned
to the other's house at an hour which is reasonable for their well being at the
end of each of the children's visits with then;

11.3.13 Both parties agree that he above agreement concerning access
only comes into force if they can not reach satisfactory arrangements between
themselves.  So long as both parties agree they may make any interim agreements
they so desire.

17.2     The parties agree that now that this agreement has been
reached, if any subsequent disputed arise between them, which they're unable to
resolve between themselves, they will seek mediation before legal action.

17.4     The parties elect to have Quebec as their residence and
because proceedings have started in Quebec they elect to have its statutes
regulate their provisional and final divorce judgments and any proceedings that
may be instituted at a later date.

17.5     The parties agree to deposit the judgement that they will
receive from the Quebec justice system, where necessary, with any competent
court so as to give to this agreement in that jurisdiction.»

[
15
]

On January 24, 2002, the Court gave act to
paragraphs 1 to 12.14 inclusively of the consent signed by the parties and
ordered them to act accordingly. This judgment was renewed thereafter on
various occasions.

[
16
]

In the circumstances the Court will spell out
later in the present judgment, said written consent and agreement was in fact
repudiated by V... shortly thereafter: as of May 31, 2002, applications where
made to the court, without mediation taking place in the first place as per
article 17.2 of the agreement, to vary custody and the terms and conditions on
access or to obtain different specific orders from the Court.

[
17
]

On May 31, 2002, V... introduced a motion for
full custody – change of custody and interim order asking the court, by
judgement on merits, to:

GRANT
full custody to Petitioner (S... V...) of two minor children for
their best interest;

GRANT
visitation rights to Respondent (N... B...) as follows:

Every second weekend, from Friday
6pm to Sunday 6pm:

ORDER
provisional execution notwithstanding appeal;

THE WHOLE, WITH COSTS

[
18
]

On June 12, 2002, V... amended her previous
motion for full custody – change of custody and interim order to conclude as
follows:

BY JUDGEMENT ON MERITS:

GRANT the present motion;

GRANT full custody to Petitioner
(V...) of the two minor children of the parties;

GRANT
visitation rights to Respondent (B...) as follows:

- Every second weekend, from Friday 6pm to Sunday 6 pm,

- Summer vacation: two full weeks with prior notice of 30 days;

-Christmas Holidays, as decided between children;

- Father's day;

ORDER Respondent (B...) to pay an
alimentary pension for the minor children in accordance with La Loi facilitant
le paiement des pensions alimentaires;

ORDER that the said alimentary
pension for the children will be paid directly to the Ministère du Revenu;

ORDER that the said alimentary
pension will be indexed on the 1
st
January of each year in
accordance with the
Civil Code of Quebec
;

ORDER the Respondent (B...) to pay
the Petitioner (V...) a monthly alimentary pension for herself of $400.00 as in
the agreement because of her little revenues and that the said pension will be
review yearly;

ORDER the Respondent (B...) to pay
the alimentary pension directly to the Ministère du Revenu;

ORDER that the said alimentary
pension for the Petitioner (V...) will be indexed each year in accordance with
the
Civil Code of Quebec
;

ORDER the Respondent (B...) to give
Petitioner (V...) a copy of his incomes in the month of February of each year
and incomes tax returns the month of April each year;

ORDER Respondent (B...) to stop
harassing or intimidating Petitioner (V...);

ORDER provisional execution
notwithstanding appeal;

THE WHOLE, with costs.

[
19
]

On November 1, 2002 B... made a motion for
interim order and asked the court to:

PERMIT
the applicant (B...) to leave the country to go back to Pakistan;

PERMIT
the applicant (B...) to bring the children with him to Pakistan;

ORDER
the attorney of the defendant and the defendant (V...) to provide
all identification cards, passports and necessary documentations to cross
Canadian borders, to the attorney of the applicant (B...), in the 24 hrs
following the present judgment;

ORDER
immediate execution of the present judgment, without standing
appeal;

THE WHOLE
without costs except in the case of contestation.

[
20
]

On November 11, 2002 B... amended his motion for
interim order and provisional measures as follows:

GRANT

the applicant (B...) full custody of the children;

GRANT
the defendant (V...) supervised access rights;

PERMIT
the applicant (B...) to leave the country to go back to Pakistan;

PERMIT
the applicant (B...) to bring children with him to Pakistan;

ORDER
the attorney of the defendant and the defendant (V...) to provide
all identifications cards, passports and necessary documentations to cross
Canadian borders, to the attorney of the applicant (B...), in the 24hrs
following the present judgment;

ORDER
immediate execution of the present judgment, without standing
appeal;

THE WHOLE
without costs except in the case of contestation.

[
21
]

On November 12, 2002, V... re-amended her motion
for provisional measures and full custody concluding that by judgment to
intervene, the court:

GRANT Defendant (V...) full custody
of both children;

REJECT Applicant's (B...) motion as
to permission to leave the country to go back to Pakistan and to bring the
children to Pakistan;

ORDER immediate execution of the
present judgement without standing appeal;

THE WHOLE without costs, except in
case of contestation.

[
22
]

On November 12, 2002, B... presented a motion to
suspend the perception of the child support and the alimony asking the court
to:

SUSPEND
the perception of the child support, paid by the applicant (B...)
for his children;

SUSPEND
the perception of the alimony paid to the defendant (V...) by the
applicant (B...);

SUSPEND
the perception of all arrears of child support and alimony;

REFER
the question of the cancellation of all the arrears of child
support and alimony to the Judge that will hear the divorce on the merit;

REFER
the question of the fixation of alimony for the defendant and child
support to the Judge that will hear the divorce on the merit;

RESERVE
the right of the parties to refer the present file to a Judge on
provisional measures, if the financial situation of the parties has change;

THE WHOLE
without costs except in the case of contestation.

[
23
]

The Court is seized of the following motions to
which this judgment will apply:

•

Motion of B... for provisional measures dated
August 15, 2001;

•

Motion of V... for full custody dated May 31,
2002;

•

Amended motion of V... for full custody dated
June 12, 2002;

•

Motion of B... for interim order dated November
1, 2002;

•

Amended motion of B... for interim order and
provisional measures dated November 11, 2002;

•

Re-amended motion of V... for provisional
measures and full custody dated November 12, 2002;

•

Motion of B... to suspend the perception of the
child support and the alimony dated November 12, 2002.

[
24
]

In their testimony, both B... and V... have
acknowledged or said that:

•

The work permit of B... expires on November 30
2002;

•

Said work permit, which allows the family to
stay legally in Canada, will not be renewed given a reorganization of the
corporation B... was working for.  B... was let go in May 2002.  He has not
find another employment since;

•

The family's immigration file is pending in
Mexico. The family has been selected by Quebec and it seems that its chances to
obtain a favourable decision are good.  Still, there is a medical issue not yet
resolved:  latent tuberculosis has been diagnosticized to Sh...- he has been
seen at Sainte-Justine Hospital- he is taking medication and appropriate
follow-up has been, and will be made, but the outcome will not be known before
January 2003. Until then, the immigration file will not progress;

•

No other demand has been made to the Canadian
immigration authorities or is pending before them.

[
25
]

The context before the Court is therefore the
following.  B... and V... had planned to immigrate to Canada with their
children.  Their separation was not to change such plan (see agreement signed
between them on January 24, 2002). B... lost his employment and has not yet
find another one.  As of November 30 next, B... will no longer have a valid
work permit.  The family will not be permitted to stay legally in Canada – They
will have to leave.  The only country where they know they can go, earn a
living and get some help from family members is Pakistan.

ISSUES before the Court

[
26
]

The issues before this court are:

•

custody and access to the children;

•

financial support (spouse alimony and child
support).

[
27
]

The Court is mainly concerned with issues of
custody and access.  A proper starting point, then, is to spell out the
provisions of the
Divorce Act
and of the
Quebec Civil code
which are relevant
to a discussion of custody and access:

Divorce Act

16. (1) A court of competent jurisdiction may, on
application by either or both spouses or by any other person, make
an
order respecting the custody of or the access to, or the custody of and access
to, any or all
children of the marriage.

[…]

(5)
Unless
the court orders otherwise, a spouse who is granted access
to a child
of the marriage
has the right
to make inquiries, and to be given
information, as to the health, education and welfare of the child.

(6) The court
may make an order under this section
for a definite or indefinite period
or until the happening of a specified event
and may impose such other
terms, conditions or restrictions in connection therewith as it thinks fit and
just.

(7) Without
limiting the generality of subsection (6), the court
may include

in an order under this section
a term requiring any person
who
has custody of a child of the marriage and who
intends to change the
place of residence
of that child to notify, at least thirty days before
the change or within such other period before the change as the court may
specify, any person who is granted access to that child
of the change,
the time at which the change will be made and the new place of residence of the
child
.

(8) In making
an order under this section, the court shall
take into consideration only
the best interests of the child
of the marriage as determined by
reference to the condition, means, needs and other circumstances of the child.

(9) In making
an order under this section, the court
shall not take into consideration
the past conduct
of any person
unless the conduct is relevant to
the ability
of that person
to act as a parent of a child
.

(10) In making
an order under this section,
the court shall give effect to the principle
that
a child of the marriage
should have as much contact

with each spouse as is consistent with the best interests of the child and, for
that purpose, shall
take into consideration the willingness
of
the person for whom custody is sought
to facilitate such contact
.
(our underlines)

17. (1) A court
of competent jurisdiction may make an order varying, rescinding or suspending,
prospectively or retroactively,

(
a
) a
support order or any provision thereof on application by either or both former
spouses; or

(
b
) a
custody order or any provision thereof on application by either or both former
spouses or by any other person.

[…]

(3) The court may include in a
variation order any provision that under this Act could have been included in
the order in respect of which the variation order is sought.

[…]

(5) Before the court makes a
variation order in respect of a custody order, the court shall satisfy itself
that there has been a change in the condition, means, needs or other
circumstances of the child of the marriage occurring since the making of the
custody order or the last variation order made in respect of that order, as the
case may be, and, in making the variation order, the court shall take into
consideration only the best interests of the child as determined by reference
to that change.

(6) In making a variation order,
the court shall not take into consideration any conduct that under this Act
could not have been considered in making the order in respect of which the
variation order is sought.

[…]

(9) In making a variation order
varying a custody order, the court shall give effect to the principle that a
child of the marriage should have as much contact with each former spouse as is
consistent with the best interests of the child and, for that purpose, where
the variation order would grant custody of the child to a person who does not
currently have custody, the court shall take into consideration the willingness
of that person to facilitate such contact.

CIVIL CODE OF QUEBEC

Art. 32

Every child has a right to the
protection, security and attention that his parents or the persons acting in
their stead are able to give to him.

Art. 33

Every decision concerning a child
shall be taken in light of the child's interests and the respect of his rights.

Consideration is given, in addition
to the moral, intellectual, emotional and material needs of the child, to the
child's age, health, personality and family environment, and to the other
aspects of his situation.

Art. 513

Separation from bed and board does
not deprive the children of the advantages secured to them by law or by the
marriage contract.

The rights and duties of fathers
and mothers towards their children are unaffected by separation from bed and
board. (which also applies in divorce matters)

Art.
514

The
court, in granting separation from bed and board or subsequently, decides as to
the custody, maintenance and education of the children, in their interest and
in the respect of their rights, taking into account the agreements made between
the spouses, where such is the case. (which also applies in divorce matters)

Art. 599

The father and mother have the
rights and duties of custody, supervision and education of their children.

They shall maintain their children.

Art. 600

The father and mother exercise
parental authority together.

If either parent dies, is deprived
of parental authority or is unable to express his or her will, parental
authority is exercised by the other parent.

Art. 604

In the case of difficulties
relating to the exercise of parental authority, the person having parental
authority may refer the matter to the court, which will decide in the interest
of the child after fostering the conciliation of the parties.

Art. 605

Whether custody is entrusted to one
of the parents or to a third person, and whatever the reasons may be, the
father and mother retain the right to supervise the maintenance and education
of the children, and are bound to contribute thereto in proportion to their
means.

Art. 612

Decisions concerning the children
may be reviewed at any time by the court, if warranted by circumstances.

[
28
]

These provisions have been interpreted by the
Supreme Court of Canada.  Here are some of the Court's teachings:

Gordon v. Goertz (1996)

«When
parents separate, one typically enjoys custody of the child, the other access.
So long as both parents live in the same area, this arrangement protects the
child's continuing relationship with both parents. However, if the custodial
parent decides to move away and change the principal residence of the child,
the situation may change. The access parent may be unable to see the child as
often as before, if at all. He or she may seek a review of the custody order,
contending that removing the child from its familiar surroundings and
restricting or depriving the child of access to the other parent is not in that
child's best interests. With the prevalence of separated families and the
increasing mobility of modern society, such applications are more common.

[…]

The principles which govern an
application for a variation of an order relating to custody and access are set
out in the
Divorce Act
. The Act directs a two-stage inquiry. First, the
party seeking variation must show a material change in the situation of the
child. If this is done, the judge must enter into a consideration of the merits
and make the order that best reflects the interests of the child in the new
circumstances.

[…]

The law can be summarized as
follows:

The parent applying for a change in
the custody or access order must meet the threshold requirement of
demonstrating a material change in the circumstances affecting the child.

If the threshold is met, the judge
on the application must
embark on a fresh inquiry into what is in the
best interests of the child, having regard to all the relevant circumstances

relating to the child's needs and the ability of the respective parents to
satisfy them.

This inquiry is based on the
findings of the judge who made the previous order and evidence of the new
circumstances.

The inquiry does not begin with a
legal presumption in favour of the custodial parent, although the custodial
parent's views are entitled to great respect.

Each case turns on its own unique
circumstances. The only issue is the best interest of the child in the
particular circumstances of the case.

The focus is on the best interests
of the child,
not the interests and rights of the parents.

More particularly the judge should
consider,
inter alia
:

(a)  the existing custody arrangement
and relationship between the child and the custodial parent;

(b)  the existing access arrangement
and the relationship between the child and the access parent;

(c)   the desirability of maximizing
contact between the child and both parents;

(d)

the views of the child;

(e)   the custodial parent's reason for moving,
only
in the
exceptional case where it is relevant to that parent's ability to meet the
needs of the child;

(f)    disruption to the child of a change in custody;

(g) disruption to the child consequent
on removal from family, schools, and the community he or she has come to
know.»(our underlines)
1

Willick
v Willick (1994)

«As against the parties, the
agreement operates as strong evidence that at the time each accepted its terms
as adequately providing for the needs of the children.»
2

W.(V.)
v. S.(D). (1996)

«67  More specifically,
it is generally recognized that the concept of custody includes,
inter alia
,
the right to determine the child's place of residence as a necessary attribute
of custody.

[…]

80    The
only criterion

that governs decisions about a child in custody proceedings, as in any other
proceedings concerning the child, is stated in art. 30
C.C.L.C.

(now art. 33
C.C.Q.
), which I have already quoted:
"the
child's interest and the respect of his rights"
.

81    In
C. (G.) v.
V.-F. (T.)
,
supra
, which considered the conditions for awarding
custody of a child to a third person in Quebec civil law, Beetz J., for the
Court, stated the following about the scope of art. 30
C.C.L.C.
, at
p. 269:

The
child's
interest has become the cornerstone of
decisions concerning it in
Quebec civil law. The reform of family law introduced in 1980 by the adoption
of the
Act to establish a new Civil Code and to reform family law
,
S.Q.
1980, c. 39
, has made the child's interest paramount. The rule that the
child's interest must prevail was for the first time unequivocally recognized
in the
Civil Code
with that reform. . . .

According
to Beetz J., "[t]here can be no question that art. 30
C.C.L.C.

applies to custody matters" (p. 271). Thus, as I wrote in
P. (D.)
v. S. (C.)
,
supra
, at p. 174: "Accordingly, whether
rights of custody or access are involved, the child's best interests as set out
in art. 30
C.C.L.C.
will be the
sole guide
". (Emphasis
in original.)

82     Authors
and courts are unanimous in this regard. Professor Mireille D. Castelli,
Le
nouveau droit de la famille au Québec: projet de Code civil du Québec et Loi
sur le divorce
(1993), at p. 225, states that the only criterion that
applies in custody matters is that of the child's interests, as set out in
art. 33
C.C.Q.
or, in the case of divorce,
s. 16
of the
Divorce
Act
. Professor Ouellette,
supra
, at pp. 225-26, noted that
while the criteria for awarding custody to a parent are many and varied, [TRANSLATION] "[t]he entire process is
concerned with the child's best interests, the only absolute criterion".
More specifically, where a child is removed and a conflict of jurisdictions
arises, it is recognized that, once the jurisdiction of Quebec courts to rule
on the child's custody has been established, the court must be guided by the
best interests of the child and must not concern itself with the law of the
child's domicile (Castel,
supra
, at p. 245; Groffier,
supra
,
at p. 144). » (our underlines)
3

Catholic Children's Aid Society of Metropolitain Toronto c. M(C.)
(1994)

«In
King v. Low, supra
, at
p. 101, McIntyre J. held:

. . .
the dominant consideration to which all other considerations must remain
subordinate must be the welfare of the child. . . . The welfare of the child
must be decided on a consideration of these and all other relevant factors,
including the general psychological, spiritual and emotional welfare of the
child. It must be the aim of the Court, when resolving disputes between rival
claimants for the custody of a child, to choose the course which will best
provide for the healthy growth, development and education of the child so that
he will be equipped to face the problems of life as a mature adult. Parental
claims must not be lightly set aside, and they are entitled to serious
consideration in reaching any conclusion. Where it is clear that the welfare of
the child requires it, however, they must be set aside.

These
concerns apply in matters of guardianship, as well. (See
New Brunswick (Minister of Health and Community Services) v. C.
(G.C.)
,
1988 CanLII 34 (SCC)
, [1988] 1 S.C.R. 1073, at p. 1079.)

Among
the factors in evaluating the best interests of a child, the emotional
well-being of a child is of the utmost importance, particularly where the
evidence points to possible long-term adverse consequences resulting from the
removal of the child from his or her foster family and the return to his or her
birth parents. The focus of maintaining family units is only commensurate as
long as it is in the best interests of the child, otherwise it would be at
cross-purposes with the plain objectives of the Act, as Wilson J. noted in
Racine
v. Woods
,
supra
, at p. 185:

. . .
it is the parental tie as a meaningful and positive force in the life of the
child and not in the life of the parent that the court has to be concerned
about. As has been emphasized many times in custody cases, a child is not a
chattel in which its parents have a proprietary interest; it is a human being
to whom they owe serious obligations.

Finally,
it is clear that the
best interests of a child require different
solutions over time
and such interests may have to take precedence over
any parental interests. As was recently said in
Young v. Young
,
supra
,
at p. 60, the "furtherance and protection of the child's best interests
must take priority over the desires and interests of the parent". Further,
as examined in
New Brunswick (Minister of Health and Community Services) v.
S.G. and S.A.
(1989),
1989 CanLII 160 (NB CA)
, 100 N.B.R. (2d) 357, at p. 360, a child's best
interests must take precedence over all other considerations including the
effect of delay:

While
it is correct to say there were administrative delays in the processing of the
guardianship application in this case, there is no proof that the delays were
deliberate or that there was any bad faith on the part of anyone involved in
the proceedings. Moreover it is to be observed that the trial judge never lost
sight of the fact that the sole issue before him was to determine what was in
the "best interest" of the child S.G. Jr.

Other
cases which have reached similar conclusions include:
Langille v. Children's
Aid Society of Halifax
, N.S.C.A., June 18, 1993, unreported;
Winnipeg
Child & Family Services v. F.(A.C.)
(1992),
1992 CanLII 13086 (MB CA)
, 42 R.F.L. (3d) 337 (Man.
C.A.), and, most recently,
Tearoe v. Sawan
, B.C.C.A., Victoria Registry
No. V01916, August 19, 1993, unreported. » (our underlines)
4

P.(D.) v. S.(C.) (1993)

«Similarly, in
Droit de la
famille -- 425
,
[1988] R.J.Q. 159
, the Superior Court had to rule on the
custody of a child and rights of access. Reeves J. eloquently expounded on
the view of the child's interests as proposed by art. 30
C.C.L.C.
,
from which I find it useful to quote large extracts (at pp. 161-62):

[TRANSLATION]  The solution to this
dilemma is to be found in an objective assessment of the various specific
aspects of this abstract notion of "the child's interest". This
assessment has to be made in conjunction with that of the parents' interests,
though without being subordinate to the latter. . . .

The
child's interest is not defined by law: it is only mentioned in art. 30
C.C. . .

. . .

It
can be said that the interest of a human being is nothing but the measure of
his welfare (
In re Goyette: Centre de services sociaux du Montréal
métropolitain
,
[1983] C.S. 429
).
There are generally four aspects to a
person's welfare: the physical or material, the emotional, the intellectual or
educational, and, finally, the moral and
religious
or spiritual aspects. The combination of all these aspects gives a person what
may be called his particular "culture"
.

The
second paragraph of art. 30 alludes to these aspects in part and by way of
illustration.

. . .

Marital
or family disputes result simply from the inability of parents and/or children
to adapt to the occurrence, unforeseen in time and space, of the innumerable
possible combinations of these four aspects of human activity.

. . .

Children,
who are destined to become fully developed human beings, stable and responsible
citizens, will survive their parents. The survival of children and, by
extension, of society is thus the underlying reason for
the priority given
to the interests and rights of the child over its parents' interests and
rights. Article 30 C.C. uses the phrase "determining factors":
this is synonymous with "priorities"
. [Emphasis added.]»
5

Young c. Young (1993)

«The power of the custodial parent
is not a "right" with independent value which is granted by courts
for the benefit of the parent, but is designed to enable that parent to
discharge his or her responsibilities and obligations to the child. It is, in
fact, the child's right to a parent who will look after his
or her best interests.

It has long been recognized that
the custodial parent has a duty to ensure, protect and promote the best
interests of the child. That duty includes the sole and primary responsibility
to oversee all aspects of day to day life and long-term well-being, as well as
major decisions with respect to education, religion, health and well-being.

The rationale for granting this
authority to the custodial parent is described by Gendreau J.A. in
Dussault
v. Ladouceur
(1987),
1987 CanLII 876 (QC CA)
, 14 R.F.L. (3d) 185 (Que. C.A.), at p. 191, as
follows:

[TRANSLATION] It goes without saying that as
a general rule, when custody of a child is granted to one parent, he or she
then exercises all the attributes of parental authority and the other parent
does not normally interfere in the custodial parent's way of doing things,
except in the exercise of his or her supervising role. The child's unity of
development is preserved in this manner and any scatterings or dislocations
that might be harmful to him or her are avoided.

The traditional decision-making
power of the custodial parent recognized by law is intimately connected to the
welfare of the child, as the need for a secure and constant source of parental
responsibility in the life of the child is well understood among those who are
knowledgeable in the psychology of children.

As Goldstein, Freud and Solnit
stress, an important function of the law on divorce or separation is to
reinforce the remainder of the family unit so that children may get on with
their lives with as little disruption as possible.

It is now widely assumed to be
self-evident in the child's best interests to ensure the non-custodial parent's
involvement in the life of the child. One result of these changes has been the
emergence of joint custody awards which are predicated explicitly on equality
of parental responsibilities and the belief that children's interests are
served by maximizing the involvement of both parents in decisions concerning the
child.

From the era in which the
enforcement of paternal rights was at the forefront of the courts' concern,
through a time where the merits of each parent's claims were weighed, we have
now reached the point where the sole question to be determined in custody and
access arrangements is the best interests of the child. Indeed, the legislation
makes it quite explicit that
only
the best interests of the child as
they are comprehensively understood should be considered in such
adjudications.»

which recognizes the need to
make the best interests of the child the primary consideration in all actions
concerning children, including legal proceedings.

everything V... has said during the hearing or written in her proceedings. The
Court believes that V... went trough difficult moments while living with B...
but not to the extent she has described.

[
100
]

It is obvious to the Court that V... has a
tendency to exaggerate or to alter her position if she feels it is in her
interest to do so. Even if at first glance she looks fragile and weak, V... has
a strong personality and she knows what she wants. No tears during her
testimony but a lot of self-control.

[
101
]

During the court hearing (November 12 to
November 15) she has explained how regular and serious were the physical
abuses. She went back to the first day of her marriage. In her affidavit dated
may 31 2002 she wrote, at paragraph 7 :
" The Respondent (B...) has an
abusive attitude towards me in front of children
going as far as
calling
me BITCH and therefore I ask by interim order the Court to order Respondent to
stop harassment, intimidation
"

(our underlines). Going as far
as calling her BITCH, even if unacceptable before her children, is far from
hitting or smacking her.

[
102
]

Since 1996, she has never gone to a shelter: she
did it for the first time on November 7, 2002. Rather than keeping this
information confidential, V...  asked the person in charge to testify before
the Court. Why, if not to try to catch or fire the Court's imagination ?

[
103
]

She has discussed at length with Sh... the
differences between shared custody and full custody : the Court does not
approve her doing so. Sh... was perturbed and he said so when he was asked by
the youth protection delegates why he did not want to visit with his mother :
she is asking too many questions was his answer. His teacher, who can be
described as a complete independent observer, wrote in the reports of February
2002 and may 2002 the following (exhibit RV-5):

«EXTRAITS PIÈCE RV-5

Date: 2002-02-08

Nom:                N...

Prénom:           SH...

Il y a eu un gros relâchement à cette étape
de la part de Sh... dû à un grand manque de concentration!

Ce qui n'a pas amélioré les choses!

C'est bien dommage car il est capable
d'excellents résultats! Reprends-toi vite avant que cela ne cause de gros
dommages»

«Date:  2002-05-10

Une toute petite amélioration à cette étape, mais pas assez pour
rattraper le retard occasionné par son relâchement.  Fais
attention!»

[
104
]

The Court feels that V... has been asking the
children to take sides. In her motion dated June 12 2002, she has written, at
paragraph 15:
" The children
are opposed
to seeing father so
often, and they want to spend more time mother"
(our underlines). The
children have clearly and spontaneously expressed the contrary to the youth
protection delegates.

[
105
]

As early as May 31 2002, V... did introduce into
the court record a motion to obtain full custody  and to limit access of the children
to their father. Why ? For the sake of the children? In their best interest or
in hers ? The Court can not find compelling reasons, either in V...'s motion or
in the proof that was made before her, for V... to set aside so easily the
agreed upon shared custody. The Court can not  accept that she was doing it in
the best interest of the children.

[
106
]

Being forced to do things is part of V...'s way
of describing events. When she was asked why she had agreed to shared custody
if B... was, as she was saying, always abusing her or why was the expression
"at a reasonable hour" in the consent if B... was always bossing her
around?  Her answer was: the mediator was well aware of the situation but,
notwithstanding these well known facts, he recommended shared custody. She was
forced to agree to the shared custody  was her saying. The Court can not accept
it happened this way.

[
107
]

V... testifies that B... has made no efforts to
find new employment in Montreal: her perceptions are wrong.

[
108
]

During her testimony before the Court she said
that B... had not been in contact with his mother since they had left Pakistan.
In her affidavits dated May 31 2002 and June 12, 2002 she wrote:
"…His
attitude is so abusive that he is telling lies and destroying Petitioner's
(V...)

good reputation in Pakistan. The  Petitioner
(B...)
is calling his mum
in Pakistan and telling lies about Petitionner
(V...)…
."

[
109
]

During her testimony before the Court she said
she had never left the children alone, unattended for. In her affidavit dated
April 9, 2002, she wrote at paragraph 15:
"
THAT
it is true that
the respondent
(V...)
has left the children unattended on several
occasions due to the fact that she had to work and due to the fact that the
petitioner
(B...)
has not paid one half of the cost of daycare as
indicated, leaving the respondent
(V...)
unable to pay said
amount."

[
110
]

Her family (mother, father and one of her
brother) are actually in Pakistan even if her parents are planning to come to
the United States by the end of the year, her father's health permitting. She
has never said she would not, or could not go to Pakistan:  she told the Court
that if she had to go she would not go with B....

[
111
]

In cross-examination or in response to questions
from the Court, V... was forced to admit that the children were doing well and
that their behaviour was good under the shared custody system (from July 1,
2001 up to August 22, 2002). She told to the Court that Sh...'s position as to
the possibility for him and his sister to go to their mother's place for an upcoming
week-end was: we have planned to go to Kirkland cinemas with friends to see the
new Harry Potter movie- if you can drive us there we might go but we really do
not want to miss this happening. Her answer was she could not drive them there
since she had no car but that they could do something else. She told the Court
she could not understand why cinema was more important for her children than
seeing their mother. Well, kids are kids! Harry Potter is Harry Potter!

[
112
]

The Court is convinced that V... cares a lot for
her children and that she is going through very difficult times balancing her
interests and ambitions or projects for the future with the children's
interests. She has not succeeded to convince the Court that, in the bests
interests of the children, she should be granted full custody of the children.

[
113
]

The Court has no reason to suspect bad faith,
fraud or sinister intentions from the part of B.... It seems to the Court that,
on the contrary, the evidence points out to his intention to get back to Canada
and have Quebec courts finally adjudicate the divorce. B... has done exactly
what the law expected him to do that is ask the permission of the Court to go
to Pakistan with the children, if need be.

[
114
]

The Court has to take into consideration the agreement
between the parties and the youth protection director (exhibit R-4) .

[
115
]

There is no proof before the Court which could
lead the Court to doubt the parental capacity of B.... To the contrary, all
witnesses have confirmed how good a father he is. Neither in her various
affidavits nor in her testimony at hearing, has V... questioned or contested
B...'s parental capacity.

[
116
]

The Court finds B...'s testimony credible.

[
117
]

He has never exaggerated, he has never
criticized V..., he has refrain himself from involving the children into the
conflict.  The Court can not conclude, at the invitation of V..., that he would
be alienating the children.

[
118
]

He has searched  seriously for new employment
hoping he could find one and renew legally his work permit : exhibits R-7 and
R-10 are concrete proof of his efforts to find employment  and to stay with his
family in North America.

[
119
]

His motions to the Court for permission to leave
Canada and for a change of custody were presented at the last minute: he did
not asked for a change of custody until November 11, 2002.

[
120
]

When V... left him in January 2001, he did not
go after her as it could be expected a violent person would do. He took the
children to the L…'s place where they stayed for few days. After they had gone
through first shock,  he organised himself and went back home with the
children.

[
121
]

He is deeply involved in his community and in
various found raising and awareness activities to eliminate discrimination
against woman and to protect women's and children's rights (exhibit R-14).

[
122
]

The Court has good reasons to believe that B...
will act in the best interests of the children and that he will follow the
Court's ruling and the Supreme Court of Canada's teachings as hereinabove cited
.

[
123
]

Given the actual situation of the parties and
their children, the Court will grant B...'s motion of November 12, 2002 as per
its conclusions, except for costs.
